title: Mainstream Klezmer: “Nigun and Hora & Freylekh”—Prelude and Fugue No.12, Book II
content_blocks: A nigun (literally “tune”) is a liturgical warm-up tune, often somewhat repetitious and sung to nonsense syllables (such as “bim-bam,” “oy-yoy-yoy,” or “aye-yay-yay”), often found in Chasidic Jewish practice. Here it serves a purpose similar to a doyna: as a warm-up or introduction. “Nigun” is also the name of the middle movement of Ernest Bloch’s Baal Shem: Three Pictures of Hassidic Life for violin and piano. I figured that if Bloch could treat a nigun with romantic excess, so could I…and so I did, my most traditionally romantic keyboard writing ever.

The Nigun is followed by a pair of dances:  a Hora and a Freylekh.  A traditional Hora (literally “dance”) is in a triple meter, often with the first beat slightly stretched.  It typically leads to a more upbeat duple meter dance, such as a “Bulgar” or—as it does here—a “Freylekh” ( “merry tune”), which typically start slow and speed up to the end.  Since both the Hora and the Freylekh tunes are treated fugally, this produces a type of double fugue (see <u>Single, Double and Triple Fugues: an Explainer</u>, August 2, 2025)—another absurd juxtaposition of stylistic extremes.

As with the other Klezmer pair (see Klezmer Sorrow and Joy, August 7, 2025), the piano has been prepared to make it sound a bit like an Eastern European zither. Here, I took a long pull-chain (as might be used to turn a ceiling fan off and on) and lay it across the ends of the strings. This is a risky preparation—the chain can bounce around and move! If it moves toward the center of the string the buzzy noise will dominate the sound, while if it moves to the very end or off the string the buzz will disappear. (Here, as with Number 9, the music can performed without the preparations.)

These pieces were inspired in part by The Cantor (also called The Rabbi with the Red Beard) and The Marriage, The Bedeken (also called Klezmer in Town) by the Ukrainian-born Parisian artist Emmanuel Mané-Katz (1894-1962). The Cantor depicts a religious figure whose singing is ready to burst forth in celebratory song, while The Marriage, The Bedeken shows the musical celebration following a wedding (a “Bedeken,” also called a “Chuppah,” is the tent-like covering under which the bride and groom get married).

To best convey the vocal origin of a nigun, I decided to enlist a singer—and what could be better than a cantor to fill the role of a cantor? Cantor Marcus Feldman joined David Kaplan for the recording of the Nigun prelude, while David perfectly captured the coexistence of the fugal seriousness and the Hora playfulness…with a cameo by me playing an additional bass line (imagine the bass player of a Klezmer quartet) in the rapidly accelerating Freylekh!
It’s the meeting of a Klezmer quartet with Bach fugues.
